title: The Danger of a Single Story
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
blurb: A TED talk about how stereotypes are made and kept alive. Adichie uses her own stories to challenge the assumptions we make about other people.
source: Extract from TED Talk about the power of storytelling
heading: The Danger of a Single Story - Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie

paragraphs.html: I'm a storyteller. And I would like to tell you a few personal stories about what I like to call "the danger of the single story." I grew up on a university campus in eastern Nigeria. My mother says that I started reading at the age of two, although I think four is probably close to the truth. So I was an early reader, and what I read were British and American children's books.

I was also an early writer, and when I began to write, at about the age of seven, stories in pencil with crayon illustrations that my poor mother was obligated to read, I wrote exactly the kinds of stories I was reading: all my characters were white and blue-eyed, they played in the snow, they ate apples, and they talked a lot about the weather, how lovely it was that the sun had come out.
Now, this despite the fact that I lived in Nigeria. I had never been outside Nigeria. We didn't have snow, we ate mangoes, and we never talked about the weather, because there was no need to. ...

What this demonstrates, I think, is how impressionable and vulnerable we are in the face of a story, particularly as children. Because all I had read were books in which characters were foreign, I had become convinced that books by their very nature had to have foreigners in them and had to be about things with which I could not personally identify.

Now, things changed when I discovered African books. There weren't many of them available, and they weren't quite as easy to find as the foreign books. But because of writers like Chinua Achebe and Camara Laye, I went through a mental shift in my perception of literature. I realized that people like me, girls with skin the colour of chocolate, whose kinky hair could not form ponytails, could also exist in literature. I started to write about things I recognized.

Now, I loved those American and British books I read. They stirred my imagination. They opened up new worlds for me. But the unintended consequence was that I did not know that people like me could exist in literature. So what the discovery of African writers did for me was this: it saved me from having a single story of what books are.

I come from a conventional, middle-class Nigerian family. My father was a professor. My mother was an administrator. And so we had, as was the norm, live-in domestic help, who would often come from nearby rural villages. So, the year I turned eight, we got a new house boy. His name was Fide. The only thing my mother told us about him was that his family was very poor. My mother sent yams and rice, and our old clothes, to his family. And when I didn't finish my dinner, my mother would say, "Finish your food! Don't you know? People like Fide's family have nothing." So I felt enormous pity for Fide's family.

Then one Saturday, we went to his village to visit, and his mother showed us a beautifully patterned basket made of dyed raffia that his brother had made. I was startled. It had not occurred to me that anybody in his family could actually make something. All I had heard about them was how poor they were, so that it had become impossible for me to see them as anything else but poor. Their poverty was my single story of them.

Years later, I thought about this when I left Nigeria to go to university in the United States. I was 19. My American roommate was shocked by me. She asked where I had learned to speak English so well, and was confused when I said that Nigeria happened to have English as its official language. She asked if she could listen to what she called my "tribal music", and was consequently very disappointed when I produced my tape of Mariah Carey.
She assumed that I did not know how to use a stove.

What struck me was this: she had felt sorry for me even before she saw me. Her default position toward me, as an African, was a kind of patronizing, well-meaning pity. My roommate had a single story of Africa: a single story of catastrophe. In this single story, there was no possibility of Africans being similar to her in any way, no possibility of feelings more complex than pity, no possibility of a connection as human equals. ...

So, after I had spent some years in the U.S. as an African, I began to understand my roommate's response to me. If I had not grown up in Nigeria, and if all I knew about Africa were from popular images, I too would think that Africa was a place of beautiful landscapes, beautiful animals, and incomprehensible people, fighting senseless wars, dying of poverty and AIDS, unable to speak for themselves and waiting to be saved by a kind, white foreigner. I would see Africans in the same way that I, as a child, had seen Fide's family. ...

But I must quickly add that I too am just as guilty in the question of the single story. A few years ago, I visited Mexico from the U.S. The political climate in the U.S. at the time was tense, and there were debates going on about immigration. And, as often happens in America, immigration became synonymous with Mexicans. There were endless stories of Mexicans as people who were fleecing the healthcare system, sneaking across the border, being arrested at the border, that sort of thing.

I remember walking around on my first day in Guadalajara, watching the people going to work, rolling up tortillas in the marketplace, smoking, laughing. I remember first feeling slight surprise. And then, I was overwhelmed with shame. I realized that I had been so immersed in the media coverage of Mexicans that they had become one thing in my mind, the abject immigrant. I had bought into the single story of Mexicans and I could not have been more ashamed of myself.
So that is how to create a single story, show a people as one thing, as only one thing, over and over again, and that is what they become. ...

Stories matter. Many stories matter. Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign, but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize. Stories can break the dignity of a people, but stories can also repair that broken dignity.

The American writer Alice Walker wrote this about her Southern relatives who had moved to the North. She introduced them to a book about the Southern life that they had left behind. "They sat around, reading the book themselves, listening to me read the book, and a kind of paradise was regained."
I would like to end with this thought: that when we reject the single story, when we realize that there is never a single story about any place, we regain a kind of paradise.

storyteller-identity.what: Three plain words name her job before anything else about her.
storyteller-identity.effect: We trust her to tell stories well, and sense that stories will be her subject.

direct-address.quote: And I would like to tell you
direct-address.what: She speaks straight to us with 'you', and 'I would like' sounds like a polite offer.
direct-address.effect: A huge audience feels personally invited in, as if chatting with a friend.

single-story-metaphor.quote: the danger of the single story
single-story-metaphor.what: She gives her idea a catchy name, in quotation marks to show it is her own phrase.
single-story-metaphor.effect: 'Single story' sounds harmless, so 'danger' makes us curious to know why.

childhood-opening.quote: I grew up on a university campus in eastern Nigeria
childhood-opening.what: 'University campus' tells us straight away that her family was educated.
childhood-opening.effect: Her Africa is a place of books and learning, which some listeners may not expect.

self-deprecating.quote: although I think four is probably close to the truth
self-deprecating.what: She corrects her mother's proud claim with a gentle joke at her own expense.
self-deprecating.effect: We laugh and relax, and trust her because she refuses to exaggerate.

specific-origins.quote: what I read were British and American children's books
specific-origins.what: She names exactly where her books came from: Britain, which once ruled Nigeria, and America.
specific-origins.effect: This raises a question of power: a Nigerian child grew up on other people's stories.

vivid-detail.quote: stories in pencil with crayon illustrations that my poor mother was obligated to read
vivid-detail.what: 'Pencil' and 'crayon' show how young she was, and 'my poor mother' is a fond joke.
vivid-detail.effect: We smile at a real little girl, so the problem that follows hits harder.

ironic-revelation.quote: I wrote exactly the kinds of stories I was reading
ironic-revelation.what: 'Exactly' admits she copied the books she read with no changes at all.
ironic-revelation.effect: We see how quietly stories shape a child, who copies them without asking if they fit.

foreign-characters.quote: all my characters were white and blue-eyed, they played in the snow, they ate apples
foreign-characters.what: She lists details from foreign books, blue eyes, snow and apples, that had no place in Nigeria.
foreign-characters.effect: The list is funny, yet she has written herself out of her own stories.

humorous-detail.quote: they talked a lot about the weather, how lovely it was that the sun had come out
humorous-detail.what: She gently mocks the British habit of chatting about the weather.
humorous-detail.effect: Humour lets her make a serious point without lecturing us.

contrast-transition.quote: Now, this despite the fact that
contrast-transition.what: 'Despite the fact that' warns us a contrast is coming.
contrast-transition.effect: We expect a gap, so the plain fact 'I lived in Nigeria' lands clearly.

parallel-negatives.quote: I had never been outside Nigeria. We didn't have snow, we ate mangoes
parallel-negatives.what: Short, flat statements set her real life beside her stories, so 'mangoes' answers 'apples'.
parallel-negatives.effect: The swaps are so small that her own world could easily have filled a story.

matter-of-fact.quote: we never talked about the weather, because there was no need to
matter-of-fact.what: She explains, deadpan, that Nigerians never discuss the weather because it hardly changes.
matter-of-fact.effect: The British habit now looks odd, showing that 'normal' depends on where you live.

lesson-statement.quote: What this demonstrates, I think, is how impressionable and vulnerable we are in the face of a story
lesson-statement.what: She steps back to state her lesson, and 'I think' stops her sounding preachy.
lesson-statement.effect: 'Vulnerable' suggests stories can hurt us, so we wonder which ones shaped us.

universal-truth.what: She adds that children are most at risk, widening her story to every child.
universal-truth.effect: Everyone listening was once a child, so we think back to our own books.

cause-effect.quote: Because all I had read were books in which characters were foreign, I had become convinced that books by their very nature had to have foreigners in them
cause-effect.what: 'By their very nature' shows she believed foreign characters were a rule of books.
cause-effect.effect: Her logic makes sense, but narrow reading has led her to a false belief.

turning-point.quote: Now, things changed when I discovered African books
turning-point.what: 'Now' and 'things changed' mark a clear shift, caused by finding African books.
turning-point.effect: The tone lifts with hope: the cure for a single story is more stories.

cultural-references.what: She names two real African novelists, including the famous Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe.
cultural-references.effect: The names back up her claim and give listeners new writers to look up.

mental-shift.quote: I went through a mental shift in my perception of literature
mental-shift.what: 'Mental shift' and 'perception' are thinking words: her whole idea of books changed.
mental-shift.effect: We see that new stories change how we think, deeply and for good.

identity-imagery.quote: girls with skin the colour of chocolate, whose kinky hair could not form ponytails
identity-imagery.what: She describes girls like herself with exact, loving details of skin and hair.
identity-imagery.effect: These warm images answer the blue-eyed characters she once wrote, so we share her joy.

transformation.quote: I started to write about things I recognized
transformation.what: A short, simple sentence sums up the change: she now writes about her own life.
transformation.effect: Seeing herself in books gives her the confidence to tell her own stories.

balanced-view.quote: Now, I loved those American and British books I read. They stirred my imagination. They opened up new worlds for me
balanced-view.what: She praises the foreign books in a tricolon (three short sentences in a row).
balanced-view.effect: Because she is generous first, we accept her criticism more readily.

but-pivot.quote: But the unintended consequence was that
but-pivot.what: 'But' turns to the problem, and 'unintended' shows nobody meant any harm.
but-pivot.effect: She blames no one: the trouble was that these were the only books she had.

thesis-statement.quote: it saved me from having a single story of what books are
thesis-statement.what: The colon builds up to her key phrase, now applied to her own life.
thesis-statement.effect: 'Saved' suggests rescue from danger, showing how much was at stake.

contextual-norm.quote: And so we had, as was the norm, live-in domestic help
contextual-norm.what: 'As was the norm' tells listeners that live-in help was ordinary for families like hers.
contextual-norm.effect: Her plain tone shows another side of Nigerian life and sets up Fide's story.

single-detail.quote: The only thing my mother told us about him was that his family was very poor
single-detail.what: 'The only thing' stresses how little she knew about Fide: just that his family was poor.
single-detail.effect: We watch one fact become a whole identity, inside her own home.

mother-voice.quote: Finish your food! Don't you know? People like Fide's family have nothing
mother-voice.what: She quotes her mother exactly, and the exclamation and question sound like a real, cross parent.
mother-voice.effect: We smile at a familiar line, yet 'have nothing' passes on a single story.

emotional-response.quote: I felt enormous pity for Fide's family
emotional-response.what: 'Enormous' is an intensifier (a word that makes a feeling stronger).
emotional-response.effect: Pity is her only feeling for the family, and it quietly places them below her.

beautiful-basket.quote: a beautifully patterned basket made of dyed raffia that his brother had made
beautiful-basket.what: The closing words, 'his brother had made', stress who made this beautiful object.
beautiful-basket.effect: Beauty and skill clash with 'poor', and her single story starts to crack.

startled.what: Three words state her surprise, standing out after the long description of the basket.
startled.effect: We feel her jolt: she had never imagined this family could be skilled.

realisation.quote: It had not occurred to me that anybody in his family could actually make something
realisation.what: She admits a thought she is not proud of, and 'actually' shows her disbelief.
realisation.effect: Her honesty makes us check our own assumptions about other people.

single-story-poverty.quote: so that it had become impossible for me to see them as anything else but poor
single-story-poverty.what: 'Impossible' and 'anything else' are absolute words: her mind had no room for another view.
single-story-poverty.effect: We see how a single story shrinks real people to one label.

conclusion-fide.quote: Their poverty was my single story of them
conclusion-fide.what: A short sentence sums up the Fide story, and 'my' shows she takes the blame.
conclusion-fide.effect: This first full example trains us to spot the same pattern later.

time-transition.quote: Years later, I thought about this when
time-transition.what: 'Years later' moves us from childhood in Nigeria to university in America.
time-transition.effect: We see the pattern repeat: the same mistake can happen anywhere.

roommate-shocked.quote: My American roommate was shocked by me
roommate-shocked.what: Now Adichie causes the shock, because she does not fit her roommate's idea of Africans.
roommate-shocked.effect: We see the single story from the other side, as she learns how being judged feels.

ironic-fact.quote: Nigeria happened to have English as its official language
ironic-fact.what: 'Happened to have' is deliberately casual, since English is official in Nigeria because of British rule.
ironic-fact.effect: The calm tone makes the roommate's surprise look silly and badly informed.

tribal-music.what: The quotation marks show these are her roommate's words, which Adichie does not accept.
tribal-music.effect: 'Tribal' suggests something primitive, as if Africa were stuck in the past.

mariah-carey.quote: I produced my tape of Mariah Carey
mariah-carey.what: Her answer to 'tribal music' is an American pop star, and the real name makes it funny.
mariah-carey.effect: We laugh, because Adichie likes the same pop music as her roommate.

stove-assumption.quote: She assumed that I did not know how to use a stove
stove-assumption.what: This assumption gets a paragraph to itself, stated flatly with no comment.
stove-assumption.effect: Left alone, the idea looks absurd, and she trusts us to see the insult.

struck-me.what: The phrase and colon tell us an important point is coming.
struck-me.effect: The talk shifts from funny stories to explaining them, so we pay closer attention.

default-position.quote: she had felt sorry for me even before she saw me. Her default position toward me, as an African, was a kind of patronizing, well-meaning pity
default-position.what: 'Default position' is a computer phrase, like a setting nobody chose, so the pity came before they met.
default-position.effect: 'Well-meaning' beside a word for talking down shows that kindness can still insult.

roommate-conclusion.quote: My roommate had a single story of Africa: a single story of catastrophe
roommate-conclusion.what: Repeating 'a single story' after the colon narrows Africa to one word.
roommate-conclusion.effect: 'Catastrophe' sums up how Africa is often shown abroad, and mirrors her story of Fide.

no-possibility.quote: no possibility of Africans being similar to her in any way, no possibility of feelings more complex than pity, no possibility of a connection as human equals
no-possibility.what: 'No possibility' opens three phrases in a row, which is called anaphora.
no-possibility.effect: It feels like doors slamming shut, with 'human equals' as the final loss.

understanding.quote: I began to understand my roommate's response to me
understanding.what: 'Began' shows that understanding her roommate took years.
understanding.effect: She models the empathy she wants from us, which makes her sound fair.

hypothetical.quote: If I had not grown up in Nigeria, and if all I knew about Africa were from popular images
hypothetical.what: Two 'if' clauses imagine a life where she knew Africa only from 'popular images'.
hypothetical.effect: Nobody can feel superior: anyone could believe this story if it was all they saw.

stereotypes-list.quote: beautiful landscapes, beautiful animals, and incomprehensible people, fighting senseless wars, dying of poverty and AIDS, unable to speak for themselves and waiting to be saved by a kind, white foreigner
stereotypes-list.what: The long list ends with a 'kind, white foreigner' as hero, mocking the usual Western picture.
stereotypes-list.effect: Africans in this story are left 'unable to speak for themselves'.

parallel-fide.quote: I would see Africans in the same way that I, as a child, had seen Fide's family
parallel-fide.what: She links her roommate's view of Africans to her own view of Fide's family.
parallel-fide.effect: Single stories are a human habit: even an African child had one about Africans.

admission.quote: But I must quickly add that I too am just as guilty in the question of the single story
admission.what: 'Must quickly add' shows she is keen to admit she makes the same mistake.
admission.effect: The talk stops feeling like an attack: if she errs, any of us can.

synonymous.what: 'Synonymous' means having the same meaning, so in the news 'immigration' came to mean 'Mexicans'.
synonymous.effect: A huge topic shrinks to one group, and 'as often happens' suggests a media habit.

endless-stories.quote: endless stories of Mexicans as people who were fleecing the healthcare system, sneaking across the border, being arrested at the border
endless-stories.what: 'Endless' shows the stories never stopped, and every action listed, such as 'fleecing' (cheating), is negative.
endless-stories.effect: Repeated often enough, these stories become the single story of a whole people.

guadalajara.quote: watching the people going to work, rolling up tortillas in the marketplace, smoking, laughing
guadalajara.what: She lists everyday actions: working, rolling tortillas, smoking, laughing.
guadalajara.effect: Ending on 'laughing' breaks the media picture and shows people like anyone else.

surprise-shame.quote: I remember first feeling slight surprise. And then, I was overwhelmed with shame
surprise-shame.what: Her feelings grow in two steps, from 'slight surprise' to being 'overwhelmed with shame'.
surprise-shame.effect: We follow her from noticing her mistake to judging herself hard for it.

media-immersion.quote: I had been so immersed in the media coverage of Mexicans that they had become one thing in my mind, the abject immigrant
media-immersion.what: 'Immersed' suggests being underwater in news, and 'abject' means hopeless and miserable.
media-immersion.effect: Even someone who knows the danger can soak up a single story without noticing.

ashamed.quote: I could not have been more ashamed of myself
ashamed.what: 'Could not have been more' means her shame was total.
ashamed.effect: Because she admits her single story so openly, we find it easier to admit ours.

how-to-create.quote: So that is how to create a single story
how-to-create.what: 'So' draws a conclusion from her examples, as she explains how a single story is made.
how-to-create.effect: After the examples, we now understand the process behind them.

repetition-show.quote: show a people as one thing, as only one thing, over and over again
repetition-show.what: 'One thing, as only one thing' and 'over and over again' repeat themselves.
repetition-show.effect: The sentence does what it describes: a single story is built by repetition.

become.quote: and that is what they become
become.what: A short, blunt clause completes the recipe, with 'become' as the key word.
become.effect: It is chilling to hear that people shrink to fit the story told about them.

stories-matter.what: Two short sentences repeat 'stories matter', and the second adds 'many'.
stories-matter.effect: The drumbeat sticks, and 'many' sums up her whole message.

dispossess-malign.quote: Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign
dispossess-malign.what: 'Dispossess' means to take what people own, and 'malign' means to speak badly of them.
dispossess-malign.effect: These formal words make stories sound like weapons that harm whole groups.

but-stories.quote: but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize
but-stories.what: 'But' turns to hope, and the sentence copies the shape of the one before.
but-stories.effect: If stories can hurt, they can also heal, and we can choose which to tell.

dignity.quote: Stories can break the dignity of a people, but stories can also repair that broken dignity
dignity.what: This is antithesis (opposite ideas side by side): 'break' and 'repair'.
dignity.effect: Ending on 'repair' leaves us with hope that stories can undo harm.

walker-quote.quote: They sat around, reading the book themselves, listening to me read the book, and a kind of paradise was regained
walker-quote.what: She quotes the American writer Alice Walker, whose 'paradise was regained' echoes Milton's poem Paradise Regained.
walker-quote.effect: A book about home brings Walker's relatives joy, proving stories can heal.

ending-thought.quote: I would like to end with this thought
ending-thought.what: 'I would like to end' mirrors 'I would like to tell you' from her opening.
ending-thought.effect: The echo rounds the talk off, and her warm, personal tone returns.

reject-single.quote: when we reject the single story, when we realize that there is never a single story about any place
reject-single.what: Two clauses begin with 'when', building to her final point, and 'never' is absolute.
reject-single.effect: We get a clear, shared task: reject single stories and look for many.

paradise-regained.quote: we regain a kind of paradise
paradise-regained.what: She borrows 'paradise' from Walker and ends the talk on it.
paradise-regained.effect: 'Regain' suggests getting back something lost, so the talk ends in hope.

impressionable.meaning: Easily influenced, so your ideas are shaped by what you see and hear.

raffia.meaning: Fibre from palm leaves, used to weave baskets, hats and mats.

patronizing.meaning: Talking down to someone as if they are less able, even while seeming kind.

overview.heading: Why Adichie gave this talk
overview.intro: Her aims build from personal stories to a call for change.

points.label: To challenge stereotypes
points.text: "how impressionable and vulnerable we are" shows how easily stories shape what we believe about others.

points.label: To teach through her own life
points.text: "I wrote exactly the kinds of stories I was reading" uses her childhood to make the lesson easy to relate to.

points.label: To inspire change
points.text: "we regain a kind of paradise" ends with hope and a clear action: reject the single story.

overview.heading: Who she is speaking to
overview.intro: She shapes her talk for several kinds of listener.

points.label: TED audience
points.text: "And I would like to tell you" speaks directly to a large, educated, international audience.

points.label: Readers of African writers
points.text: "Chinua Achebe and Camara Laye" shows how widely she reads and gives others new writers to discover.

points.label: Anyone who has stereotyped others
points.text: "I too am just as guilty" includes herself, so nobody feels singled out for blame.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Her voice moves from warm and funny to honest and ashamed.

points.label: Storyteller's warmth
points.text: "I'm a storyteller" opens the talk with a friendly, simple tone.

points.label: Self-mocking humour
points.text: "four is probably close to the truth" makes her seem honest and likeable.

points.label: Shocked realisation
points.text: "I was startled" shows real surprise at her own assumption.

points.label: Deep shame
points.text: "I could not have been more ashamed of myself" is a brave, open admission.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Her techniques make the ideas clear and memorable.

points.label: Central metaphor
points.text: "the danger of the single story" names the idea that runs through the whole talk.

points.label: Specific imagery
points.text: "skin the colour of chocolate" uses warm, physical detail to show her joy at being represented.

points.label: Repetition for emphasis
points.text: "Stories matter. Many stories matter." builds a strong rhythm that sticks in the mind.

points.label: Anaphora (repeated openings)
points.text: "no possibility" opens three phrases in a row, shutting out every kind of connection.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The talk moves through her life, one lesson at a time.

points.label: Chronological order
points.text: She moves from childhood in Nigeria to university in America, then to Mexico, and finds the same lesson in each place.

points.label: Parallel examples
points.text: Her childhood view of Fide's family mirrors her roommate's view of Africa, so the two stories echo each other.

points.label: Building to confession
points.text: "I too am just as guilty" comes after we have watched others judge her, so her honesty surprises us.

points.label: Circular ending
points.text: "we regain a kind of paradise" echoes the Alice Walker quotation and ends on hope.

journey.title: Adichie's Journey: From Single Story to Multiple Narratives

stages.desc: A Nigerian child writing about snow and apples
